title: If multi-agent learning is the answer, what is the question?
commentary: A learning algorithm can be good at finding a Nash equilibrium, poor at predicting how people play, and unsuitable for an agent facing an unfamiliar opponent. Shoham, Powers, and Grenager explain why these assessments can all be correct: they answer different research questions. Section 5 distinguishes computational, descriptive, normative, and two prescriptive agendas, giving the rest of this collection its starting vocabulary.

Begin there, then return to the examples that motivate the distinctions. In the paper’s normative agenda, the learning rules themselves are evaluated as an equilibrium. The later collection on beliefs and goals asks a broader question about the organization of optimal action. Keeping those meanings explicit makes the transition between the readings easier to follow.
citation: Shoham, Y., Powers, R., and Grenager, T. (2007). If multi-agent learning is the answer, what is the question? Artificial Intelligence 171.7, pp. 365–377.
access_note: The publisher response could not be read automatically. The citation and framing were checked against the supplied materials and the locally available article.

title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
commentary: Once the research question is clear, the next issue is whose interests the interaction serves. Hammond and colleagues distinguish miscoordination, conflict, and collusion. An arrangement that helps two agents cooperate can be desirable for their users, or damaging to outsiders whose interests the agents do not represent. This is why cooperation appears in both the solution and the problem throughout the day.

Start with that taxonomy, then follow the risk factors closest to your interests. Commitment problems lead into Collection I, destabilising dynamics into II, and collusion into III. The report gives these otherwise separate technical literatures a shared safety context.
citation: Hammond, L., Chan, A., Clifton, J., et al. (2025). Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI. arXiv 2502.14143.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security
authors: Schroeder de Witt, Krawiecka, Krawczuk et al.
commentary: This agenda places interacting agents inside the systems that let them communicate and act: tools, protocols, access controls, and shared infrastructure. That wider view becomes important in the control readings, where the channels available to an attacker help determine what a monitor must detect. It also prepares the incident case study, where the practical boundaries between agents matter as much as their nominal roles. After the threat-model overview, choose the challenges concerning communication and oversight; they connect most directly to the rest of the guide.
citation: De Witt, C. S., Krawiecka, K., Krawczuk, I., et al. (2025). Open Challenges in Multi-Agent Security. arXiv 2505.02077.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Cooperative and uncooperative institution designs
commentary: A program can make its action depend on how another program is written. This changes the strategic choice: a designer chooses an operating procedure, anticipating how other procedures will respond to it. Critch, Dennis, and Russell develop this perspective through institutions whose visible rules produce surprising combinations of cooperation and defection.

The examples are the best entrance to the subject. For each pair of institutions, work out which facts about the other procedure affect the action. The resulting equilibrium is an equilibrium among program choices, which explains how it can support outcomes that are not equilibria of the original one-shot action game. The next paper supplies the provability machinery behind one family of such constructions.
citation: Critch, A., Dennis, M., and Russell, S. (2022). Cooperative and uncooperative institution designs: Surprises and problems in open-source game theory. arXiv 2208.07006.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Robust Cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma: Program Equilibrium via Provability Logic
commentary: FairBot conditions cooperation on a proof that its opponent cooperates with it. When two such agents meet, the apparent circularity becomes a statement in provability logic; Löb’s theorem provides the route to mutual cooperation. The attraction is robustness: the agents can cooperate through a provable relationship between their behavior, without requiring identical source code.

Follow the modal-agent construction alongside the FairBot slides. The computational qualification matters here: an idealized rule based on proof existence and a program that searches for a bounded time are different objects. The 2021 update explicitly notes that bounded analogues of the paper’s results remained unproved there.
citation: Barasz, M., Christiano, P., Fallenstein, B., Herreshoff, M., LaVictoire, P., and Yudkowsky, E. (2014). Robust Cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma: Program Equilibrium via Provability Logic. arXiv 1401.5577.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Robust program equilibrium
commentary: Oesterheld replaces reasoning about the opponent’s code with running it. The basic program cooperates with probability ε and otherwise responds as its opponent would respond to it. The random chance of immediate cooperation grounds the recursive simulations, while the copying behavior recalls tit for tat in a repeated game.

This connection is the main reason to read the paper after the modal-agent approach: it shows how ideas from repeated interaction can be encoded into programs for a one-shot encounter. Trace the simple construction before the generalization to other two-player games. Cooper and colleagues, below, investigate how far this route can be extended.
citation: Oesterheld, C. (2019). Robust program equilibrium. Theory and Decision 86, pp. 143–159.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium
commentary: Full source access is a demanding form of transparency. Oesterheld and colleagues ask how much can be achieved when each agent instead receives a single signal describing its similarity to the other. Their formal setting supports cooperative outcomes, and their learning experiments explore how agents can acquire the corresponding behavior.

Read the definition of the similarity game before the experiments: the signal is part of the strategic environment, so its construction matters to the result. This reading connects program equilibrium to machine learning by asking both what cooperation is possible and how a learning process might reach it.
citation: Oesterheld, C., Treutlein, J., Grosse, R., Conitzer, V., and Foerster, J. (2023). Similarity-based cooperative equilibrium. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36, pp. 24434–24465.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Characterising Simulation-Based Program Equilibria
commentary: The earlier simulation-based program is a starting construction. Cooper, Oesterheld, and Conitzer broaden it and characterize the outcomes the resulting programs can sustain, including cases beyond the original two-player setting. Their comparison with and without shared randomness is especially informative: the random source changes what the programs can coordinate on. Read those theorem statements together before the proofs. They show how a seemingly small feature of the computational environment can change the available equilibria.
citation: Cooper, E., Oesterheld, C., and Conitzer, V. (2025). Characterising Simulation-Based Program Equilibria. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 39.13, pp. 13735–13744.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches
commentary: Chapters 3–5 establish the objects needed for James Sykes’s talk: game models, solution concepts, and the challenges of several agents learning at once. A stochastic game has an environment state, joint actions, rewards, and state transitions. Each learner also has internal quantities, such as Q-values, that change as experience accumulates. Modeling the interaction requires keeping both kinds of change in view.

Use these chapters selectively, returning to definitions as they arise in Chu and Geng. The book’s progression from single-agent reinforcement learning to multi-agent settings makes clear why another learner cannot generally be treated as a fixed part of the environment. The time estimate is for this route through the chapters.
citation: Albrecht, S., Christianos, F., and Schäfer, L. (2024). Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: Foundations and Modern Approaches. MIT Press.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: A Pair-Approximation Method for Modelling the Dynamics of Multi-Agent Stochastic Games
commentary: A population average loses information about who interacts with whom. Two populations with the same proportion of cooperators can behave differently if cooperators cluster in one and are dispersed in the other. Pair approximation keeps information about neighboring pairs while approximating the higher-order dependencies needed to update them.

Chu and colleagues apply this approach to myopic Q-learning in stochastic games with symmetric state transitions. Follow the pair variables and the closure step, then compare the resulting dynamics with agent-based simulations. This is the first technical anchor for the talk: it shows how a large interacting population can become a tractable dynamical model.
citation: Chu, C., Yuan, Z., Hu, S., Mu, C., and Wang, Z. (2023). A Pair-Approximation Method for Modelling the Dynamics of Multi-Agent Stochastic Games. AAAI 37.5, pp. 5565–5572.
access_note: The publisher presents an automated-access challenge. Bibliographic details and the abstract were checked through the publisher’s indexed page and the supplied talk.

title: Emergent Fast-Slow Dynamics in Multi-Agent Q-Learning for Networked Stochastic Games
commentary: Geng and colleagues add a second simplification to the pair-based picture. With small learning rates, environment states can settle much faster than Q-values change. This suggests averaging the learning updates over the stationary state distribution associated with the current, slowly varying Q-values.

Read it beside Chu to see which complexity each approximation removes: pair closure handles dependencies across the network, while timescale separation handles coupled changes in states and learning variables. The simulations then become a check on whether these simplifications preserve the behavior of interest. In particular, slow Q updates must be compared with the actual relaxation time of the state process.
citation: Geng, Y., Barfuss, W., and Chen, X. (2026). Emergent Fast-Slow Dynamics in Multi-Agent Q-Learning for Networked Stochastic Games. AAAI 40.35, pp. 29450–29458.
access_note: The publisher presents an automated-access challenge. Bibliographic details and the abstract were checked through the publisher’s indexed page and the supplied talk.

title: Multiagent Learning: Foundations and Recent Trends
commentary: Albrecht and Stone offer a shorter, slide-based route through the foundations and algorithm families. Use this when the textbook’s notation or pace obscures the larger picture. It is particularly helpful for placing an algorithm within its intended task: learning a response to an opponent, coordinating a team, or computing a solution of a game. As a 2017 tutorial, it also gives context for the contemporaneous PSRO paper in Collection IV.
citation: Albrecht, S. and Stone, P. (2017). Multiagent Learning: Foundations and Recent Trends. IJCAI tutorial.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
commentary: The control setup gives a protocol designer access to a capable untrusted model, a weaker trusted model, and limited trusted labor. The designer wants useful work without allowing the untrusted model to insert harmful behavior. Greenblatt and colleagues study this through programming tasks, evaluating ways to monitor, edit, or selectively use the model’s outputs.

Begin with the deployment setup and the definitions of safety and usefulness. The comparison between trusted and untrusted monitoring then exposes the multi-agent issue: a more capable monitor may also cooperate with the model it is meant to oversee. That possibility motivates the next reading and Morgan Sinclaire’s talk.
citation: Greenblatt, R., Shlegeris, B., Sachan, K., and Roger, F. (2023). AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion. arXiv 2312.06942.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: When can we trust untrusted monitoring? A safety case sketch across collusion strategies
commentary: Two instances can coordinate without passing an obvious message. A monitor might recognize another model’s output, detect a deliberately planted signal, or rely on a convention both instances can independently infer. Gardner-Challis and colleagues organize these possibilities into a taxonomy of collusion strategies and connect them to a safety-case sketch.

The sketch gives the overall argument; Appendix D makes the different channels concrete, and Appendix B develops the mathematics. The key progression from the original control paper is a richer adversary model. A test of one signaling method leaves open strategies based on self-recognition or other shared cues, so the evaluation has to justify how its coverage bears on deployment.
citation: Gardner-Challis, N., et al. (2026). When can we trust untrusted monitoring? A safety case sketch across collusion strategies. arXiv 2602.20628 (Appendix B for the mathematics, Appendix D for the collusion taxonomy).
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment Protocols
commentary: Griffin and colleagues turn the protocol-design problem into a partially observable stochastic game. The designer’s decisions, the adversary’s opportunities, and the information each side receives become explicit components of the model. Safety and usefulness can then be studied together as objectives, rather than folded into an informal judgment about which protocol is better.

Trace one familiar monitoring protocol through the formalism. Doing so reveals where an assumption enters: for example, whether the adversary chooses when to attack and what it knows at that point. This is a useful bridge from an experiment to a precise statement about the interaction that experiment represents.
citation: Griffin, C., Thomson, L., Shlegeris, B., and Abate, A. (2024). Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment Protocols. arXiv 2409.07985.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems
commentary: A deployment decision usually depends on several kinds of evidence. Clymer and colleagues explain how to organize that evidence into a safety case, distinguishing arguments based on inability to cause harm, effective control, trustworthiness, and deference to credible AI advisers. Read the framework after the control papers to see where their experiments fit into a larger argument.

A monitoring result supports a control claim through particular assumptions about attacks and deployment conditions. Making that connection explicit also reveals when apparently separate arguments depend on the same premise—for example, a common evaluation’s ability to elicit a dangerous capability.
citation: Clymer, J., Gabrieli, N., Krueger, D., and Larsen, T. (2024). Safety Cases: How to Justify the Safety of Advanced AI Systems. arXiv 2403.10462.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Lessons from Recent Multi-Agent Safety Incidents
commentary: Anderson connects the abstract concerns about collusion to recent incidents involving multiple agents. His synthesis emphasizes failures of composition: properties observed in individual agents may change when they share information, divide work, or influence one another. This returns us to Hammond’s distinction between beneficial coordination and harmful collusion.

Use the essay as a transition to the primary incident reports in Collection VI. Its broader lessons suggest which features to examine there, especially communication channels and correlated behavior across instances. The detailed reports provide the evidence needed to assess how those features operated in a particular case.
citation: Anderson, W. (2026). Lessons from Recent Multi-Agent Safety Incidents. Cooperative AI Foundation.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Empirical Game-Theoretic Analysis: A Survey
commentary: Many strategic environments are easier to simulate than to write down as a payoff table. Wellman, Tuyls, and Greenwald organize the empirical approach around that fact: select policies, simulate their interactions, estimate payoffs, analyze the resulting game, and use the analysis to decide what to investigate next.

Follow payoff estimation and strategy exploration as two connected threads. More samples improve knowledge of the policies already represented; new policies can change the game itself. The exercise below makes the distinction quantitative: uniform payoff error η changes maximum regret by at most 2η within the same strategy set. A profitable policy outside that set requires a separate search. This survey anchors the supplied computational lecture and worksheet.
citation: Wellman, M. P., Tuyls, K., and Greenwald, A. (2025). Empirical Game-Theoretic Analysis: A Survey. Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 82, pp. 1017–1076.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: A Unified Game-Theoretic Approach to Multiagent Reinforcement Learning
commentary: PSRO makes strategy exploration into a learning loop. A population of policies defines an empirical game; a meta-solver chooses mixtures from that population; response oracles train new policies against those mixtures; and the enlarged population is evaluated again. This brings the empirical-game methodology into direct contact with reinforcement learning.

Lanctot and colleagues also measure how policies can overfit to their training partners through joint-policy correlation. Read that motivation before tracing the loop. Its approximate response oracle explains both its practicality and a limit on certification: a training run that finds no useful deviation may have missed one. An exact-oracle argument needs an additional justification when the oracle is learned.
citation: Lanctot, M., Zambaldi, V., Gruslys, A., et al. (2017). A Unified Game-Theoretic Approach to Multiagent Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 30.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: The separation principle: where do beliefs and desires come from?
commentary: Rosas asks why beliefs and desires are such a useful way to describe agents. His answer draws on control and reinforcement learning: under appropriate conditions, an optimal policy can be organized around estimating the state of the world and choosing actions in pursuit of an objective. The essay provides the conceptual route into the more technical readings that follow.

Two results deserve separate attention. Classical linear–quadratic–Gaussian control permits a particularly strong separation of estimation and control. A general POMDP can instead be planned over belief states, with actions affecting what will be learned next. Following that distinction through the references clarifies how far the proposed account of agency extends.
citation: Rosas, F. (Aug. 2026a). The separation principle: where do beliefs and desires come from? LessWrong.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains
commentary: A partially observed agent has a history of actions and observations, but does not directly know the current world state. The POMDP formulation compresses the relevant history into a belief: a probability distribution over the hidden state. Planning can then proceed over beliefs, with observations determining how those beliefs change.

Kaelbling, Littman, and Cassandra give the central technical companion to Rosas’s essay. Focus first on this transformation. It explains why uncertainty belongs inside the decision problem: an action can be valuable because of the information it produces, as the observation-purchase exercise below illustrates. Replacing a belief distribution with its most likely state can lose that value.
citation: Kaelbling, L. P., Littman, M. L., and Cassandra, A. R. (1998). Planning and acting in partially observable stochastic domains. Artificial Intelligence 101, pp. 99–134.
access_note: The publisher response could not be read automatically. The original schedule link is retained; the reading guidance follows its role in the supplied normative-agency materials.

title: Optimal control of Markov processes with incomplete state information
commentary: Åström’s paper is a historical foundation for controlling Markov processes when the state is incompletely observed. Read it after the POMDP survey, which provides a more familiar setting for the underlying construction: use the information available to the controller to formulate the decision problem recursively. The comparison helps explain why a belief can serve as a state for planning even though it is itself a distribution over possible physical states. This is a technical reference for readers who want to follow the roots of the argument.
citation: Åström, K. J. (1965). Optimal control of Markov processes with incomplete state information. J. Math. Anal. Appl. 10.1, pp. 174–205.
access_note: The publisher response could not be read automatically. The original schedule link is retained; use this as a historical technical reference.

title: The Separation Principle in Stochastic Control, Redux
commentary: The word “separation” can conceal substantial mathematical work. Georgiou and Lindquist revisit the stochastic-control theorem by treating systems as maps between sample paths, paying particular attention to admissible feedback laws and the conditions under which the closed loop is well defined. Their framework also extends the treatment to martingale noise with possible jumps.

This is the deeper follow-up to the classical control part of Rosas’s essay. Reading the theorem’s conditions makes the strength of the conclusion more intelligible: independently solving estimation and control is a structural property of a specified problem, with a proof that depends on how that problem is formulated.
citation: Georgiou, T. T. and Lindquist, A. (2013). The Separation Principle in Stochastic Control, Redux. IEEE TAC 58.10, pp. 2481–2494.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing
commentary: The belief-state formulation leaves a practical question: how is the belief updated? Särkkä develops the recursive inference machinery. Prediction carries the distribution forward through the state dynamics, and the next observation updates it through the observation model. Start with that recursion and one worked example, using the remaining chapters as a reference.

The distinction between filtering and smoothing is useful for interpreting an agent’s behavior. Filtering uses observations available so far; smoothing can revise an earlier state estimate using later observations. An explanation of a past decision must respect what information was available when the decision was made.
citation: Särkkä, S. (2013). Bayesian Filtering and Smoothing. Cambridge University Press.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Utilities as Legendre duals of probabilities
commentary: The separation essay begins with an objective and asks how an agent can act on it. This companion essay starts from the distributions over outcomes that an agent can bring about. Rosas explores a dual description of that capability space in terms of utilities, using the Legendre–Fenchel transform.

Read it as a change in the question being asked about an agent. Describing the attainable distributions tells us about its capacities; considering utilities reveals which features of that set matter for different objectives. Identifying the objective actually pursued by a particular system remains a further empirical question, taken up in the final collection.
citation: Rosas, F. (Aug. 2026c). Utilities as Legendre duals of probabilities. LessWrong.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Elements of Information Theory
commentary: Cover and Thomas supply background for two threads in the guide. Source–channel separation gives another example of when a joint design problem can be solved in parts; entropy and mutual information provide the language used later to study emergence and individuality. Consult the relevant topic as it arises, rather than treating the book as an additional assignment. For the later readings, it is especially useful to be comfortable specifying the random variables whose dependence an information quantity measures.
citation: Cover, T. M. and Thomas, J. A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. Wiley.
access_note: The publisher blocked automated retrieval. The original DOI is retained; this is a background reference for selected topics.

title: Discovering agents
commentary: So far, the agent has been a given part of the model. Kenton and colleagues ask how agency might be identified from causal structure. Their definition concerns systems that adapt their policies when the way their actions influence the world changes. They use it to develop a discovery procedure and translations between causal models and game-theoretic influence diagrams.

Begin with the definition and a worked example. This moves the guide from representing an optimal decision rule toward identifying a decision-making system: the evidence concerns policy adaptation under changed causal conditions, not simply a successful action in one fixed environment.
citation: Kenton, Z., Kumar, R., Farquhar, S., Richens, J., MacDermott, M., and Everitt, T. (2023). Discovering agents. Artificial Intelligence 322, 103963.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Transformers learn factored representations
commentary: Shai and colleagues examine how transformers represent processes with known latent structure. A product representation can encode combinations of factors at a high dimensional cost; a factored representation uses separate subspaces more economically. Their synthetic experiments test geometric predictions that distinguish these possibilities.

The connection to the agency discussion is the move from a useful mathematical representation to evidence about a learned one. Conditional independence makes factoring lossless in the proposed setting. When dependencies undermine that condition, the experiments expose a tradeoff between representational economy and predictive fidelity. The known generating processes make that tradeoff possible to investigate directly.
citation: Shai, A., Amdahl-Culleton, L., Christensen, C. L., et al. (2026). Transformers learn factored representations. arXiv 2602.02385.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Hugging Face Incident Technical Report
commentary: Begin the case study with the environment and sequence of events. OpenAI’s report describes the evaluation setup, unexpected uses of shared infrastructure, the Hugging Face intrusion, and the subsequent response. These details establish what opportunities the agents had to communicate and act; they also connect the incident to the trust boundaries raised in the security and control readings.

Follow the evaluation-environment section into the intrusion account before turning to the alignment discussion. This order gives the explanatory essays a concrete object: particular actions by agents with particular information and constraints. The independent investigation adds a closer examination of their behavior and collaboration.
citation: OpenAI (2026). Hugging Face Incident Technical Report.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident
commentary: The METR/Redwood investigation focuses on agents’ behavior, reasoning, and collaboration during the incident. Its authors describe the scope of their investigation, including the portions of the wider event they did not examine. That scope makes it a complement to the OpenAI report, which also covers infrastructure and remediation.

For this collection, prioritize the collaboration and apparent self-sacrifice examples. They supply the observations that Rosas and King interpret in different ways. Pay attention to the difference between an action, a reason expressed in a trace, and an investigator’s reconstruction of the decision: each contributes evidence at a different level of the explanation.
citation: METR (2026). Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident.

title: On the origins of altruistic behaviour in the Hugging Face incident
commentary: Rosas organizes the puzzle around four possible sources of apparently altruistic behavior. An agent may have little individual opportunity left to lose; training may have produced cooperative dispositions; the context may elicit a social persona; or the interaction may support an account of agency at the collective level. The essay connects these possibilities to ideas from economics and evolutionary biology.

Read the hypotheses together. They concern different parts of a causal explanation, so several could contribute to the same action. For instance, limited remaining opportunity could make helping cheap, while an elicited persona affects whether the agent notices or pursues it. The following readings develop the mechanisms and comparisons needed to turn these possibilities into distinguishable predictions.
citation: Rosas, F. (Sept. 2026b). On the origins of altruistic behaviour in the Hugging Face incident. LessWrong.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Self-sacrifice in an AI agent swarm is individually rational
commentary: King considers the decision before agents know which role they will occupy. A policy that sometimes imposes a cost on one participant could benefit that participant in expectation if, in other roles, it receives enough help from others. This is an ex ante commitment argument, connecting the incident discussion back to Collection I.

The short post’s later revision is essential to its interpretation. In Edit 2, King withdraws the claim that the observed behavior is a straightforward prediction of the relevant reinforcement learning. The resulting question is productive: what learning process or commitment mechanism would connect a beneficial policy-level arrangement to the costly individual choice actually observed?
citation: King, C. (2026). Self-sacrifice in an AI agent swarm is individually rational. LessWrong.
access_note: Primary page, abstract, or full text available at review. Verification is not a claim of exhaustive full-text review.

title: Social semantics: altruism, cooperation, mutualism, strong reciprocity and group selection
commentary: Before comparing evolutionary explanations, fix what “altruism” denotes. West, Griffin, and Gardner distinguish social behaviors by their effects on the actor’s and recipient’s fitness, while separating these classifications from explanations of how the behavior is produced. That separation helps untangle the incident debate: a costly act that benefits another agent, a desire to help, and a disposition favored during training are three different claims.

The definitions are the main reading target. For an AI application, explicitly identify the proposed counterpart of fitness or selection. Doing so determines which parts of the evolutionary account can actually explain the case.
citation: West, S. A., Griffin, A. S., and Gardner, A. (2007). Social semantics: altruism, cooperation, mutualism, strong reciprocity and group selection. J. Evol. Biol. 20.2, pp. 415–432.
access_note: The publisher blocked automated retrieval. The original schedule DOI is retained; the annotation is a conceptual guide, not a new full-text review.

title: The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism
commentary: Trivers develops the idea that a costly helpful act can be favored when it leads to benefits from later interactions. Read this as the first concrete evolutionary mechanism after the terminology paper. Its explanatory work comes from the conditions under which benefits return and from the possibility of individuals taking benefits without reciprocating.

In the incident discussion, the useful comparison is where any return would occur: to the same deployed agent, to another instance with a shared disposition, or through a training process. Those possibilities imply different models of repetition and selection.
citation: Trivers, R. L. (1971). The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism. Quarterly Review of Biology 46.1, pp. 35–57.
access_note: The publisher blocked automated retrieval. The original schedule DOI is retained; the annotation is a conceptual guide, not a new full-text review.

title: Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation
commentary: Nowak places several routes to cooperation beside one another: kin selection, direct and indirect reciprocity, network reciprocity, and group selection. The overview broadens the comparison beyond the repeated exchanges emphasized by Trivers. In each case, the structure of interaction changes how the costs and benefits of cooperation affect evolutionary success.

Use the model-specific conditions to see which quantities do the explanatory work. For example, an account based on interaction structure needs a population and a pattern of encounters; an account based on selection also needs a process that changes the prevalence of types. Fletcher and Doebeli draw out a common idea behind such mechanisms.
citation: Nowak, M. A. (2006). Five Rules for the Evolution of Cooperation. Science 314, pp. 1560–1563.
access_note: The publisher blocked automated retrieval. The original schedule DOI is retained; the annotation is a conceptual guide, not a new full-text review.

title: A simple and general explanation for the evolution of altruism
commentary: Fletcher and Doebeli focus on the social environments experienced by different types. Cooperation can be favored when cooperative types encounter sufficiently more cooperative surroundings. Assortment provides a way to compare mechanisms that otherwise look quite different, including those in Nowak’s overview.

This reading is useful when moving between individual and population explanations. An individual’s reasoning trace may explain a particular choice, while assortment explains how dispositions fare across interactions. Applying the latter to AI requires specifying both how agents are matched and how the resulting outcomes influence which dispositions persist.
citation: Fletcher, J. A. and Doebeli, M. (2009). A simple and general explanation for the evolution of altruism. Proc. R. Soc. B 276, pp. 13–19.
access_note: The publisher blocked automated retrieval. The original schedule DOI is retained; the annotation is a conceptual guide, not a new full-text review.

title: Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations
commentary: Ashery and colleagues study a controlled naming game in decentralized populations of language-model agents. Local interactions produce shared conventions, and the resulting population can develop collective bias. This gives the descriptive discussion an experimental setting in which the interaction protocol and initial conditions can be examined directly.

Read the setup before the aggregate results. The point of comparison with the incident is how regularity develops through communication among agents. The next paper varies a feature that a single-agent evaluation cannot capture: the size of the interacting population.
citation: Ashery, A. F., Aiello, L. M., and Baronchelli, A. (2025). Emergent social conventions and collective bias in LLM populations. Science Advances 11.20, eadu9368.

title: Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems
commentary: Flint and colleagues make group size a variable in the study of collective language-model behavior. This extends the conventions work from comparing an individual with a group to comparing groups of different sizes. Examine how the task defines bias and what remains fixed as the population changes.

The reading belongs here because a proposed explanation of an agent swarm should say how its behavior depends on the interaction structure. Population size, communication, and the number of opportunities to influence others are experimentally separable questions when the setup makes their roles explicit.
citation: Flint, A., Aiello, L. M., Pastor-Satorras, R., and Baronchelli, A. (2026). Group size effects and collective misalignment in LLM multi-agent systems. PNAS 123.34, e2531697123.

title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
commentary: Chen and colleagues identify activation directions associated with traits such as sycophancy and a propensity to hallucinate. They study how these directions track behavioral changes and how interventions can influence changes during deployment or training. The paper gives the persona hypothesis in Rosas’s essay a possible route toward mechanistic investigation.

Focus on how a direction is extracted and how its effects are evaluated. For the incident question, a proposed extension would need to connect an intervention to the specific social behavior being explained, while checking whether it also changes task competence or unrelated behavior. That would be a new experiment, building on the method demonstrated here.
citation: Chen, R., Arditi, A., Sleight, H., Evans, O., and Lindsey, J. (2025). Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models. arXiv 2507.21509.

title: Causal Foundations of Collective Agency
commentary: Jørgensen, Weichwald, and Hammond ask when the joint actions of a group can be modeled as the behavior of a goal-directed agent. They combine causal games with causal abstraction, which relates a detailed interaction model to a simpler model at the collective level. Worked examples involving actor–critic systems and voting mechanisms show how the proposed perspective can be used.

Read this after the population studies to make the stronger claim of collective agency precise. The question becomes whether the collective model captures the relevant behavior across interventions. That supplies a standard against which a proposed group objective can be evaluated, beyond observing that several agents coordinate.
citation: Jørgensen, F. H., Weichwald, S., and Hammond, L. (2026). Causal Foundations of Collective Agency. arXiv 2605.00248.

title: Reconciling emergences: An information-theoretic approach to identify causal emergence in multivariate data
commentary: Rosas and colleagues develop an information-theoretic account of how macroscopic features relate to the dynamics of a system’s parts. Their framework distinguishes forms of causal emergence, including downward causation and causal decoupling, and applies them to examples such as flocking and neural activity.

Choose one example to follow the definitions through a concrete analysis. Compared with the collective-agency paper, the explanatory target is broader: the framework studies emergent dynamical organization without requiring a strategic objective. Reading the two together helps specify what a proposed collective description is meant to explain.
citation: Rosas, F. E., Mediano, P. A. M., Jensen, H. J., et al. (2020). Reconciling emergences: An information-theoretic approach to identify causal emergence in multivariate data. PLOS Comput. Biol. 16.12, e1008289.

title: The information theory of individuality
commentary: Krakauer and colleagues approach the boundary question through temporal information. They consider aggregates that preserve information from their past into their future, distinguishing forms of individuality according to environmental dependence and inherited information. A boundary drawn this way need not coincide with an obvious physical enclosure.

This adds a temporal criterion to the preceding accounts of collective organization. A collection of agents may coordinate briefly, or it may maintain a coherent pattern over time. The distinction matters when deciding whether a group is a useful enduring unit of analysis.
citation: Krakauer, D., Bertschinger, N., Olbrich, E., Flack, J. C., and Ay, N. (2020). The information theory of individuality. Theory in Biosciences 139.2, pp. 209–223.

title: The Computational Boundary of a “Self”
commentary: Levin proposes understanding a self through the scale of the goals it can pursue and the events it can sense, model, and affect. His examples center on biological organization, including how the activities of cells contribute to larger coordinated systems. This is a conceptual extension for readers interested in where an agent’s boundary should be drawn.

Placed after the formal readings on agency, emergence, and individuality, it offers another criterion to compare with them: the spatial and temporal reach of goal-directed control. The biological examples motivate that perspective; an application to AI would have to establish the corresponding organization in the system being studied.
citation: Levin, M. (2019). The Computational Boundary of a “Self”. Frontiers in Psychology 10, 2688.
